summary: Segment Routing over IPv6 describes paths as sequences of segments, advertised by protocols like BGP, IS-IS, and OSPFv3. This document extends BGP Link State to advertise SRv6 segments along with their behaviors and attributes. It is similar to BGP-LS for SR over MPLS in RFC 9085.

eli5.summary: This lets a network share its map, including the special SRv6 stops, with a central planner that decides routes.

subtitle: How a network's SRv6 segments, locators and peering SIDs are reported to controllers through BGP Link State.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) nodes hold many segments and attributes, but controllers that compute paths need to learn them. BGP-LS already carried this kind of data for SR over MPLS, not for SRv6.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9514 defines new BGP-LS TLVs for SRv6 node, link and prefix attributes, plus a new SRv6 SID NLRI (type 6) with its own attribute TLVs, mostly copying fields from the IS-IS and OSPFv3 SRv6 extensions.
tldr.outcome: BGP-LS consumers such as an SR Path Computation Engine can see SRv6 capabilities, locators, End.X SIDs and BGP peering SIDs across IGP domains and Autonomous Systems.

facts.label: SID Structure lengths
facts.value: Sum must be at most 128 bits

today: RFC 9514 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2023, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the BGP-LS counterpart of the SRv6 extensions in RFC 9352 and RFC 9513.

sections.title: Why SRv6 Needs BGP-LS Support
sections.content:
SRv6 is Segment Routing instantiated on the IPv6 data plane (RFC 8402). A segment is usually referred to by its SRv6 Segment Identifier, or SID. The network programming model in RFC 8986 describes how behaviors are bound to SIDs, so a network program can be written as a combination of SIDs.

IS-IS and OSPFv3 have been extended to advertise some SRv6 SIDs (RFC 9352, RFC 9513), and other SIDs can be instantiated on a node by other means. The same kind of information for SR over MPLS is already carried in BGP-LS by RFC 9085, and for BGP Egress Peer Engineering by RFC 9086.

RFC 9514 does the equivalent for SRv6. In BGP-LS, the identifying key of each node, link or prefix goes in the NLRI, and its properties go in the BGP-LS Attribute (RFC 7752). Applications that need topology visibility can then also receive SRv6 SIDs from nodes across an IGP domain or across Autonomous Systems.
sections.eli5: Routers already tell a planner about the roads. This RFC lets them also tell the planner about the new SRv6 shortcuts and what each one does.

sections.title: Mapping SRv6 Data onto BGP-LS
sections.content:
When a BGP-LS router reports information it learned from IS-IS or OSPFv3, the SRv6 data is, in practice, a simple copy of the relevant fields from the IGP TLV or sub-TLV into the matching BGP-LS TLV. When the data comes from BGP itself (for example for EPE) or uses Direct as the Protocol-ID, it is derived from the local node and advertised only on behalf of that router.

The data is split across the three existing BGP-LS NLRI types and one new one. Node information uses the Node NLRI, link information uses the Link NLRI, and a locator uses the Prefix NLRI. Individual SIDs get a new NLRI, so that a node with many SIDs does not produce one huge update, and a change to a single SID does not force a large update message.

All new TLVs follow the formats and common field definitions of RFC 7752.
sections.eli5: Instead of stuffing every shortcut into one giant letter about a router, each shortcut gets its own small note. Changing one shortcut then means sending only one small note.

sections.title: Node and Link TLVs
sections.content:
For a node, the SRv6 Capabilities TLV (type 1038, length 4) carries a 2-octet Flags field copied from the IS-IS or OSPFv3 SRv6 Capabilities encoding and a 2-octet Reserved field. One instance MUST be included for each SRv6-capable node. The TLV is not extensible, so future extensions are expected to be top-level TLVs. SRv6 Maximum SID Depth types reuse the Node MSD TLV of RFC 8814.

For a link, the SRv6 End.X SID TLV (type 1106) advertises the SID of an IGP Adjacency SID or a BGP EPE Peer Adjacency SID. It carries a 2-octet Endpoint Behavior, 1-octet Flags, Algorithm and Weight, a Reserved octet, the 16-octet SID and optional sub-TLVs. One instance can appear per End.X SID.

The SRv6 LAN End.X SID TLV (type 1107 for IS-IS and 1108 for OSPFv3) adds a Neighbor ID, a 6-octet IS-IS System-ID or a 4-octet OSPFv3 Router-ID. It lets a node announce its adjacencies to all non-DIS or non-DR nodes on a LAN in a single Link NLRI, instead of originating one Link NLRI per neighbor. Link MSD types reuse the Link MSD TLV from RFC 8814.
sections.eli5: A router can say what it is able to do, and can name the doorway to each neighbor. On a busy street with many neighbors, it lists them all on one page.

sections.title: Locators and the SRv6 SID NLRI
sections.content:
An SRv6 SID has locator, function and argument parts (RFC 8986). A node is provisioned with one or more locators, which are covering prefixes for its SIDs. Each locator is advertised as a Prefix NLRI with the SRv6 Locator TLV (type 1162), which has Flags, Algorithm, Reserved, a 4-octet Metric and optional sub-TLVs (none are currently defined). A Prefix NLRI with a Locator TLV is also treated as a normal routing prefix only if an IGP Metric TLV (TLV 1095) is associated with it.

The new SRv6 SID NLRI (type 6) holds a Protocol-ID, an 8-octet Identifier, Local Node Descriptors and SRv6 SID Descriptors. The descriptors MUST contain a single SRv6 SID Information TLV (type 518, length 16, carrying the 128-bit SID) and MAY contain a Multi-Topology Identifier TLV.
sections.eli5: A locator is like a street name that covers many house numbers. Each individual house number, a SID, gets its own listing in a new kind of directory.

sections.title: SID Attributes, Structure and BGP Peering SIDs
sections.content:
The attributes of an SRv6 SID are carried in the BGP-LS Attribute of the SID NLRI. The SRv6 Endpoint Behavior TLV (type 1250, length 4) is mandatory and holds the Endpoint Behavior code point from the registry in RFC 8986, a Flags octet and an Algorithm octet. For SIDs from BGP EPE or Direct, no flags are currently defined, and the algorithm value MUST be 0 unless an algorithm is associated locally with the locator the SID is allocated from.

The SRv6 BGP PeerNode SID TLV (type 1251, length 12) is mandatory for SIDs advertised by BGP for EPE. It has B, S and P flags (Backup, Set, Persistent), a Weight, the 4-octet Peer AS Number and the 4-octet Peer BGP Identifier. A PeerNode SID has one instance of the TLV. A PeerSet SID has one instance per peer in the set, and the S-Flag is set.

The optional SRv6 SID Structure TLV (type 1252, length 4) gives the length in bits of the Locator Block, Locator Node, Function and Argument parts. Their sum MUST be less than or equal to 128. It can also be a sub-TLV of the End.X SID and LAN End.X SID TLVs.

Compared with SR-MPLS EPE, SRv6 needs no extra Link NLRI for each BGP session. Each PeerNode or PeerSet SID is tied to the BGP speaker node and advertised in an SRv6 SID NLRI, with peer information as attributes.
sections.eli5: Each shortcut has a label saying what it does. A BGP peering shortcut also says which neighbor it leads to, and one label can cover a whole group of neighbors at once.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned NLRI type 6 (SRv6 SID NLRI) in the "BGP-LS NLRI Types" registry. It also assigned nine TLV code points in the "BGP-LS NLRI and Attribute TLVs" registry: 518, 1038, 1106, 1107, 1108, 1162, 1250, 1251 and 1252.

A new registry, "SRv6 BGP EPE SID Flags", was created with the allocation policy "Standards Action". Bit 0 is the Backup Flag, bit 1 the Set Flag and bit 2 the Persistent Flag. Bits 3 to 7 are unassigned.
sections.eli5: The official number list now has entries for the new notes and a new list for the three peering flags.

sections.title: Manageability
sections.content:
The extensions do not affect BGP protocol operation and management beyond what RFC 7752 already discusses. The malformed-attribute syntactic checks in that document now cover the new TLVs. Checking the meaning of the TLVs, and how they relate to the NLRI types, is left to the consumer of the BGP-LS data (an application or controller) and not to BGP.

A consumer such as an SR Path Computation Engine (PCE) can use the information to learn SRv6 capabilities and SID mappings and to compute paths for traffic engineering. Encoding or decoding errors may leave the PCE without the information or with wrong information, and how the PCE handles that is implementation specific.
sections.eli5: The router just passes the notes along. It is up to the planner reading them to check that they make sense.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new extensions present a similar risk to the existing link-state information in RFC 7752, and its security considerations also apply. The IGP instances that originate the underlying data are assumed to support the security and authentication mechanisms described in RFC 9352 and RFC 9513.

SR operates within a trusted domain, and policies built from SIDs advertised via BGP-LS are expected to stay inside it. Isolating BGP-LS peering sessions is RECOMMENDED, so that topology information, including the new SR information, is not advertised to an external BGP peering session outside the SR domain.
sections.eli5: This map is for the planners inside the network only, so it should be kept away from outsiders.
